subject: system-design
title: Key-Value Store
summary: A distributed hash map you get and put by key, and the partitioning, replication, and quorum machinery that lets it scale across many nodes.

blocks.text: A key-value store is a distributed hash map: you put a value under a key and get it back later, with no schema and no joins. Because the interface is so narrow, it can spread its data across hundreds of nodes and grow by adding more. The classic design to know is Amazon's Dynamo, which trades the rich queries of a relational database for predictable scale and availability.

No single node holds every key, so keys must be split across nodes. Naive hashing with node = hash(key) mod N remaps almost every key when N changes, forcing a huge reshuffle on each add or removal. Consistent hashing instead places nodes and keys on a ring and assigns each key to the next node clockwise.

items: A key belongs to the first node found walking clockwise from its position on the ring.
Add or drop a node and only its neighbor's keys move. The rest stay put.
Virtual nodes (many ring points per physical node) even out the load and hot spots.

blocks.text: For durability, each key is copied to the next N nodes around the ring. N is the replication factor, typically three, and it sets how many machines must fail before a key is lost. Rather than always waiting for all N, the store lets you tune two numbers: W, the replicas a write must reach before it acks, and R, the replicas a read must consult. When W + R > N the read and write sets overlap, so a read is guaranteed to see the latest write. That gives strong-ish consistency without full synchrony.

blocks.title: The quorum tradeoff
blocks.text: R and W are dials, not constants. Low values give fast, highly available reads and writes but weaker guarantees; high values give stronger consistency at the cost of latency and availability when nodes are down. Keep W + R > N if you want read-your-writes.

items: Concurrent writes to different replicas can diverge into two versions of a key that must be reconciled.
Last-write-wins keeps the highest-timestamp version. It is simple, but silently drops a concurrent update.
Vector clocks track causality, detecting true conflicts so the app or a merge function resolves them without losing data.

blocks.text: With no central coordinator, nodes learn about each other through gossip: each periodically exchanges its view of the cluster with a few random peers, so membership and failure information spreads epidemically. A node that stops responding is marked down by its peers, and its requests route to the surviving replicas. Consistent hashing, N-way replication, tunable quorums, conflict resolution, and gossip together make up the Dynamo-style key-value store: a simple lookup API that scales horizontally and stays available.
